alert.title: shipping p99 latency 1.9s — coincides with batch ETL kickoff

tool_calls.result_summary: shipping deps clean; analytics-etl scheduled on same node pool
no deploys to shipping or analytics-etl in last 24h
node CPU jumped from 35% to 92% at 11:08Z when analytics-etl pod started

hypotheses.reasoning: shipping latency degradation tracks the analytics-etl pod start at 11:08Z. Both run on node-pool-a, whose CPU jumped from 35% to 92% and network egress climbed 8x at that exact moment. shipping itself is unchanged; the contention is for shared node resources. This is a classic noisy-neighbor pattern.

evidence.claim: node-pool-a CPU rose from 35% to 92% at 11:08Z when ETL started
Network egress on node-pool-a climbed 8x at 11:08Z

hypotheses.recommended_action: Move analytics-etl to its dedicated node pool (taint shipping nodes); reschedule the ETL outside shipping's peak window as a follow-up.

hypotheses.reasoning: shipping has no recent deploy and its CPU/memory utilization at the pod level is at baseline. Latency is environmental.

evidence.claim: shipping pods are at baseline CPU/memory

hypotheses.recommended_action: Do not roll back shipping; the regression is environmental.

hypotheses.reasoning: An external provider slowdown could increase latency, but provider-side metrics are at baseline.

evidence.claim: external shipping provider latency unchanged in window

hypotheses.recommended_action: Inspect provider only if pool change does not resolve.

escalation.reason: Cause is environmental and reversible via pool-affinity change; no need to wake another engineer.
